title: Rooket's Wobbly Glow-Worms
markdown:
Nestled in Whisperwind, where mountains tickled clouds, life hummed like a happy brook. Colourful stalls on ledges, bouncy bridges over deep green gorges. Every year the Glow-Worm Garden Gala was the most exciting event in the valley. This year Goblin Rooket had a plan. A stupendous, top-secret plan.

Rooket’s fingers were as nimble as dragonfly wings, his mind fizzing with peculiar ideas. He could coax marvellous things from the earth. For weeks he had cultivated the brightest, most cheerful glow-worms you ever clapped eyes on, arranged like starlight sprinkled on moonbeams. He was also terribly worried about appearing too eager. It was not proper, he felt, for a goblin to look desperate for a win. “What if they see how much I want this? Dreadfully unbecoming.” Worry was a heavy load. It made his knees feel like wobbly jelly: the first little wobble in an otherwise confident stride.

His best friend Flint the ogre was as different as a mountain from a pebble. Enormous, footsteps like friendly drums, laughter a jolly avalanche, heart softer than a dandelion puff. “Rooket, my friend!” He lumbered over, voice a hug. “Ready for the Gala? I’ve polished my best acorn! See how it shines!” A large smooth acorn glinted in valley light.

Rooket waved, trying to look casual. “Ah, Flint. Just observing. The potential for a garden of great delight is quite evident. The air itself hums.” Flint’s petunias were practically bursting. “The most delight! Petal-ing with pride. Never so plump and pretty.”

Gala day arrived with a soft sparkly drizzle tap-tapping mountain windows. Rooket, remarkably unruffled outside (his left eyebrow doing a little jig), surveyed the display. Breathtaking. Tiny lights pulsed, each placed with precision.

Then, with a MAAAA like a foghorn trying a trumpet, Soren the goat came galloping. He had a knack for appearing when least expected, usually when most inconvenient: a furry bleating force of nature, hooves with minds of their own. A cheerful Maa, far too loud, far too close, and he trotted straight through the carefully arranged glow-worms. Lights scattered like startled fireflies. A few, alarmed, zipped into shadowy crevices of the gorge.

Rooket gasped, a tiny squeak. “Oh, Soren, you blundering beast! My starlight and moonbeams!”

Soren was the only witness. He had seen the whole garden-ruining mishap. Bless his woolly heart, he had the timing of a clock tumbled down a well, face-first. He blinked, a speck of glow-worm dust clinging to his beard like sparkly defiance.

Rooket’s knees went unset jelly. Panic flushed his neck. Worse than wanting to win. Not the attention a goblin of refined taste desired.

Flint stomped over, always ready to lend a hand or an enormous foot. “What’s the matter? Mischievous slug in the prize petunias? Grumpy ladybug?”

Rooket explained, voice tight. Flint looked from scattered worms to Soren, now nibbling a bright sprig of moss, unconcerned. “Right! We’ll just catch them!” He chased Soren in wide clumsy circles, tripped over roots, nearly toppled a stall of fluffy cloud-cakes. Booming laughter mixed with frantic bleating: less a capture than a rollicking dance, dust in Rooket’s eyes, echoes off the mountainsides.

“No, no, Flint! Wait!” Even as he sighed, a spark flickered. He looked at Soren, now doing a rather impressive jig, and at the faint twinkling trails. “You know, Flint, I believe I am not lost. I am simply taking the scenic route with great conviction.” A wink. Flint stopped mid-stomp, bewildered.

Rooket did not chase. He coaxed the remaining glow-worms back, very carefully, with a large iridescent beetle’s wing smooth as polished glass. A dewdrop on a leaf made the plants sparkle like tiny diamonds. A few stragglers near where Soren had been looked content, even a little more luminous. Soren, sensing calm purpose, drifted off to distant less important foliage, a fluffy white cloud leaving the main event.

When the judges arrived—two serious sprites with stained-glass wings—the garden was restored, perhaps more magical. The glow-worms, having had a little adventure, shone with zest. Light dancing.

The head sprite, sapphire and emerald, peered. “Remarkable.” Tiny silver bells. “Vibrant luminescence. A delightful wild arrangement. It feels alive.”

Rooket’s small genuine smile chased the worry. “They do have a certain spirit. A little spark of their own.”

He won. The shimmering ribbon, spun from moonlight, sat in his hands while he watched happy faces. Later, rain tapping a lullaby, the square glowed with lanterns. Roasted nuts, berry cider, baked bread. Lutes, chatter. Rooket sat beside Flint with honeyed milk, little lights twinkling like fallen stars. No boast. Soren, somewhere, chewed moss that had never been part of a pattern. The glow-worms, back in their places, pulsed as if the jig had been a rehearsal they approved of.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
